Ross October 21, 2026 Overview & Executive Summary This technical report documents the end-to-end data harmonization, multi-stage quality control, hierarchical bio-optical modeling, and ternary partitioning workflow for “Ternary partitioning of continental scale water clarity” (Jawitz, Cohen, & Ross). Water clarity—most widely measured in situ as Secchi disk depth (\(z_{SD}\), in meters)—is governed by pure water itself (\(k_w\)) and three primary light-attenuating constituents (LACs): non-algal particles (NAP), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and phytoplankton chlorophyll a (\(\text{Chl }a\)). By combining contrast-transmittance theory (\(k_d = 1 / z_{SD}\); Lee et al. 2015, 2018) with the additive Beer–Lambert law, Secchi depth can be expressed directly in terms of constituent concentrations: \[z_{SD} = \frac{1}{k_w + \alpha_{\text{NAP}}\,\text{NAP} + \alpha_{\text{DOC}}\,\text{DOC} + \alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\,\text{Chl }a}\] Using harmonized in situ records spanning 1970–2025 across the conterminous United States from the AquaMatch Environmental Data Initiative (EDI) data suite (Brousil et al. 2024a, 2024b, 2025; De La Torre et al. 2025), this pipeline: Harmonizes and screens multi-agency Water Quality Portal (WQP) measurements (Section 1–Section 4), assembling 277,382 simultaneous four-variable training observations (Secchi + Chl a + DOC + TSS/SSC) and 478,929 simultaneous three-constituent application observations across 39,396 unique monitoring stations in U.S. streams, lakes, and estuaries. Applies a physically grounded, non-circular quality-control protocol (Section 4) that pairs standard EPA/USGS analytical reporting floors (ifelse(x < floor, floor, x) rather than marginal quantile truncation) with an a priori Beer–Lambert physical plausibility screen derived strictly from published optical cross-sections (Bannister 1974; Kirk 1994; Morris et al. 1995; Gohin et al. 2005). This screen removes the 1.44% of WQP records exhibiting severe (\(>6.3\times\)) physical discordance—such as unflagged streambed bottom hits in shallow, clear streams—while preserving 100% of true environmental extremes (Secchi up to \(13.96\text{ m}\), TSS up to \(978\text{ mg L}^{-1}\), Chl a up to \(990\ \mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)). Evaluates 10 hierarchical general linear models (Section 5–Section 7) stratified across U.S. EPA Omernik Ecoregions (Levels I–IV; Omernik & Griffith 2014) and water-body types (Estuary, Lake, Stream), achieving \(R^2 = 0.41\text{ to }0.53\) (Model 7 \(R^2 = 0.50\) across 47 Level III ecoregions) without local site-by-site calibration and demonstrating sample-size convergence for groups with \(n > 1{,}000\) (Figure S1). Partitions continental water clarity in ternary space (Section 8–Section 9), revealing distinct optical signatures across streams, lakes, and estuaries (Figure 2), river-to-estuary continuum transitions along 231 km of the Delaware River and Bay (Figure 3), and site-level temporal stability (lucistatic vs. lucidynamic regimes across 9,128 long-term stations; Figure 4). Visualizing Why Optical Partitioning & Total Visibility Matter ({sonicray} 3D GPU Simulation) Why does partitioning diffuse light attenuation (\(k_d\)) across Chl a, DOC, and NAP matter physically and ecologically—and why must ternary proportions \((f_{\text{NAP}}, f_{\text{DOC}}, f_{\text{Chl }a})\) be interpreted alongside total visibility (\(z_{SD} = 1 / k_d\))? Each constituent transforms the underwater light field and water color in a fundamentally different way: Chlorophyll a (Phytoplankton Blooms): Absorbs strongly in blue (\(440\text{ nm}\)) and red (\(675\text{ nm}\)) bands while phytoplankton cells backscatter green light (\(550\text{ nm}\)), shifting water color from deep oligotrophic blue to luminous emerald green as Secchi depth shoals. Dissolved Organic Carbon (CDOM / Brownification): Absorbs exponentially across short wavelengths with virtually zero particulate backscattering, turning lakes and rivers into dark tea-stained / mahogany blackwater where light is extinguished rapidly without mineral turbidity. Non-Algal Particles (TSS / Sediment Plumes): Strongly backscatter broadband red, yellow, and green wavelengths, turning water chalky tan / turbid ochre and driving the steepest collapse in Secchi visibility (\(z_{SD} < 0.4\text{ m}\)). Ternary proportions alone do not encode total visibility (\(z_{SD}\)): Because ternary coordinates sum to \(100\%\) (\(f_{\text{NAP}} + f_{\text{DOC}} + f_{\text{Chl }a} = 1\)), two waterbodies sitting at the exact same point in ternary space (e.g., a balanced \(33\%\text{ NAP}, 33\%\text{ DOC}, 33\%\text{ Chl }a\) mixture) can represent either an ultra-clear alpine lake (\(z_{SD} = 5.3\text{ m}\), where submerged littoral boulders are visible) or a murky eutrophic-sediment waterbody (\(z_{SD} = 0.38\text{ m}\)) when total constituent concentrations scale up. Pairing the ternary diagram with our calibrated Beer–Lambert Secchi depth model (\(z_{SD} = 1 / [k_w + \sum \alpha_i C_i]\)) resolves both who controls light attenuation (ternary composition) and how much total light is attenuated (Secchi visibility across Clear vs. Dark/Turbid states). Section 3 Partitioning Non-Algal Particles (NAP) & Method Sensitivity The additive Beer–Lambert model partitions non-water light attenuation among three mutually exclusive constituent pools: phytoplankton cells, non-algal suspended particles (NAP, comprising mineral sediments, organic detritus, and depigmented cell fragments), and dissolved organic matter (represented by DOC). Because standard gravimetric monitoring measures bulk Total Suspended Solids (TSS)—which includes both non-algal particles and living phytoplankton biomass—living algal dry mass must be subtracted from bulk TSS to isolate NAP: Optical Component Measured In-Situ Variable Model Predictor & Units Phytoplankton (\(\alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\,\text{Chl }a\)) Chlorophyll a (\(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{Chl }a\) (\(\text{mg m}^{-3} = \mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) used directly Non-algal particles (\(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}\,\text{NAP}\)) Bulk TSS / SSC (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{NAP} = \text{TSS} - \text{biomass}(\text{Chl }a)\) (\(\text{g m}^{-3} = \text{mg L}^{-1}\)) Dissolved organic matter (\(\alpha_{\text{DOC}}\,\text{DOC}\)) DOC (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{DOC}\) (\(\text{g m}^{-3} = \text{mg L}^{-1}\)) used directly Following the empirical bio-optical relationship of Gohin et al. (2005) (Remote Sens. Environ. 95:29–46), phytoplankton dry biomass (in \(\text{mg L}^{-1}\), converting \(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\) to \(\text{mg L}^{-1}\) via division by \(1{,}000\)) is estimated from \(\text{Chl }a\) (\(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) as a nonlinear power law: \[\text{biomass}_{\text{algal}}\ [\text{mg L}^{-1}] = \frac{234}{1000}\,(\text{Chl }a)^{0.57} = 0.234\,(\text{Chl }a)^{0.57}, \qquad \text{NAP} = \text{TSS} - 0.234\,(\text{Chl }a)^{0.57}\] In code, add_nap() in R/prep.R computes chl_a_biomass and stores non-algal particles in the column tss_dead. Key Bio-Optical Decisions: NAP Derivation (R/prep.R) Why \(\text{Chl }a\) is retained as the regression predictor while algal dry mass is subtracted from TSS. Algal dry mass is computed solely to remove living phytoplankton mass from bulk gravimetric TSS. Using \(\text{Chl }a\) (\(\text{mg m}^{-3}\)) directly as the third predictor in the linear regression (\(k_d - k_w = \alpha_{\text{NAP}}\,\text{NAP} + \alpha_{\text{DOC}}\,\text{DOC} + \alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\,\text{Chl }a\)) ensures that the fitted slope \(\alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\) has standard bio-optical units of \(\text{m}^2\ (\text{mg Chl }a)^{-1}\), enabling direct comparison with theoretical first-principles chlorophyll cross-sections (\(k_c \approx 0.008\text{–}0.020\text{ m}^2\ [\text{mg Chl }a]^{-1}\); Bannister 1974; Kirk 1994). Why the nonlinear Gohin et al. (2005) power law (\(0.234\,\text{Chl }a^{0.57}\)) outperforms constant linear C:Chl ratios. Intracellular carbon-to-chlorophyll ratios decline systematically from oligotrophic to eutrophic waters due to nutrient sufficiency and self-shading photoacclimation (Geider et al. 1987, 1997; Cloern et al. 1995; Gohin et al. 2005). As demonstrated in the sensitivity table below, constant linear dry-mass:Chl a ratios (100:1 or 200:1) severely over-predict algal dry mass during high-chlorophyll blooms, generating up to 31.7% non-physical negative NAP values, whereas the Gohin et al. (2005) power law produces negative NAP in only 2.02% of samples while yielding virtually identical attenuation slopes. Handling of near-zero negative NAP in training vs. application. During OLS model training (n = 275,349), the 1.66% (4,580 rows) of samples where \(0.234\,\text{Chl }a^{0.57}\) slightly exceeds measured TSS are retained without truncation so random analytical noise near zero does not bias slope estimates. Section 4 Analytical Reporting Floors & WQP Physical Plausibility Diagnostics Multi-agency observational compilations such as the Water Quality Portal (WQP) synthesize measurements from hundreds of federal, state, tribal, and local monitoring organizations. While the AquaMatch harmonization workflow standardizes parameter names, units, and analytical tiers, 1–2% of raw WQP records contain severe field-recording or data-entry anomalies that can heavily leverage ordinary least squares (OLS) regression slopes and depress explained variance (\(R^2\)) if left unscreened. At the same time, marginal quantile truncation (such as trimming the top and bottom 0.1% or 1% of each variable independently) unnecessarily discards genuine ultra-clear oligotrophic waters (Secchi up to 13.96 m) and real storm-flow sediment or algal bloom events (TSS up to 978 mg/L, Chl a up to 990 µg/L) that obey Beer–Lambert optics.
